name: Jerusalem
info: Jerusalem is a city on a plateau in the Judaean Mountains, first settled near the Gihon Spring around 3000 BCE, and holy to Judaism, Christianity and Islam, whose status is disputed today.

facts.founded: First settled near the Gihon Spring between 3000 and 2800 BCE, according to archaeological evidence; no founder is known, and the Bible says David took it from the Jebusites around 1000 BCE.
facts.where: On the southern spur of a plateau in the Judaean Mountains between the Mediterranean and the Dead Sea, in the Southern Levant, claimed as a capital by both Israel and Palestine.
facts.known: the First and Second Temples; the Western Wall; the Church of the Holy Sepulchre; the Dome of the Rock and al-Aqsa; Aelia Capitolina; the Crusader Kingdom of Jerusalem; the walls of Suleiman; sieges and conquests by many powers
facts.today: A city of over a million people whose Old City is a World Heritage Site and whose political status remains disputed between Israel and Palestine.

t: Jerusalem grew from a settlement by the Gihon Spring into a capital and sanctuary city, and was held in turn by Canaanites, Egyptians, Judahites, Babylonians, Persians, Greeks, Romans, Byzantines, Muslim dynasties, Crusaders, Mamluks, Ottomans, the British, Jordan and Israel.
It is holy to Judaism, Christianity and Islam, and many of its buildings, from the Temple Mount to the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, mark events that each faith tells in its own way.
Its history includes repeated sieges, destructions and expulsions, and the status of the city is still contested in the present.

sections.origins:
Jerusalem stands on the southern spur of a plateau in the Judaean Mountains, about 760 m above sea level in the Old City, between the Mediterranean and the Dead Sea. The Kidron, Hinnom and Tyropoeon valleys meet just south of the Old City, and the Tyropoeon once divided the lower city into two hills, the Temple Mount to the east and the rest of the city to the west. Water was always scarce, and the first settlement was tied to the Gihon Spring: archaeological evidence suggests it was established there between 3000 and 2800 BCE.

The name is variously explained as "foundation of the god Shalem", Shalem being a Canaanite god of dusk. Egyptian Execration Texts of the Middle Kingdom may refer to the city, and the Amarna letters of Abdi-Heba, from the 1330s BCE, name an Urusalim, which may be the earliest certain mention. By the 17th century BCE the Canaanites had built massive walls on the eastern side to protect the water system. In the Late Bronze Age the city was one of several small city states that were vassals of the king of Egypt. According to the Bible, it was then called Jebus and its independent Canaanite inhabitants were Jebusites; the Books of Samuel say that David took it from them and made it the City of David.
sections.growth:
The Hebrew Bible places the city's rise in the time of David and Solomon, and says that Solomon built the First Temple. Archaeologists are divided on whether the excavations support this: Eilat Mazar contends that her digging uncovered large stone buildings of the right period, while Israel Finkelstein disputes both her interpretation and the dating. Radiocarbon dates show that Jerusalem was relatively densely inhabited in the 12th to 10th centuries BCE, with a major expansion to the west beginning in the 9th century BCE. Thomas L. Thompson argues that it could act as a state capital only from the middle of the 7th century BCE, whereas Omer Sergi holds that it was already a significant city in Iron Age IIA.

Under the Hasmoneans, who ruled an independent state from Jerusalem, the number of rural production sites within a two hour walk of the Temple Mount nearly doubled, from 15 to 29. Herod the Great, who took the city in 37 BCE, rebuilt the Second Temple and more than doubled the size of the surrounding complex, so that the Temple Mount became the largest temenos in the ancient world. Pliny the Elder called Jerusalem "the most famous by far of the Eastern cities". By the end of the Second Temple period the city had, by modern estimates, 70,000 to 100,000 people, a peak that was not broken until the 20th century.
sections.rulers:
According to the Bible, Jerusalem was the capital of a united Kingdom of Israel under David, and after the kingdom divided it was the capital of Judah, which it remained for some 400 years until the Neo-Babylonian Empire captured it in 586 BCE. After the Persian conquest of Babylon in 539 BCE the Jews were allowed to return, and the city lay within the Persian province of Yehud. Alexander's conquests brought Greek rule in 332 BCE, then Ptolemaic control, and from 198 BCE Seleucid. The Maccabean revolt gave Jerusalem back as the capital of the Hasmonean state until Pompey took it in 63 BCE. Herod ruled it as a client king from 37 BCE, and direct Roman rule followed in 6 CE.

After 70 CE it became the Roman colony of Aelia Capitolina, then a Byzantine city. The Sasanians held it from 614 to 629, when Heraclius reconquered it. The Rashidun Caliphate took it in 638, followed by the Umayyads, Abbasids and Fatimids. Seljuk forces captured it in 1071, the Fatimids retook it in 1098, and the Crusaders took it in July 1099 and made it the capital of the Kingdom of Jerusalem. Saladin recaptured it in 1187, and the Mamluks held it from 1260 until 1516. The Ottomans ruled it until Edmund Allenby entered on 11 December 1917, and Britain administered it under a Mandate from 1922 to 1948.
sections.life:
Jerusalem's life has long been shaped by its holy places and the pilgrims who came to them. Under Aelia Capitolina Hadrian placed the forum at the junction of the Cardo and the Decumanus and built a temple to Jupiter Capitolinus, and Jews were banned from the city. In Byzantine times the burial remains are exclusively Christian. Benjamin of Tudela, who visited in 1173, described a small city full of Jacobites, Armenians, Greeks and Georgians, with two hundred Jews living in a corner under the Tower of David.

The Mamluks left about 90 surviving structures from the 13th to 15th centuries, among them madrasas, libraries, hospitals, caravanserais, fountains and public baths, mostly around the edge of the Temple Mount. Under Suleiman the Magnificent the walls that still define the Old City were built, and Jews, Christians and Muslims could find a synagogue, a church and a mosque on one street. In the mid-19th century the population was divided into four main communities, Jewish, Christian, Muslim and Armenian, each living mainly near its shrines. The Church of the Holy Sepulchre was partitioned among the Greek Orthodox, Catholic, Armenian, Coptic and Ethiopian churches, and its keys were kept by two Muslim families regarded as neutral. During the Mandate a rule requiring buildings to be faced with sandstone preserved the look of the city as it grew.
sections.crises:
By one count, Jerusalem has been destroyed completely at least twice, besieged 23 times, captured and recaptured 44 times and attacked 52 times. Sennacherib besieged it in 701 BCE; the Bible says an angel killed 185,000 men in his army, while Sennacherib's own account says Hezekiah was shut up like a caged bird and paid tribute. The Babylonians took it in 597 BCE and again in 586 BCE, when they burnt the Temple and destroyed the walls. In 70 CE, after a five-month siege, Titus's legions destroyed much of the city and burnt the Second Temple. After the Bar Kokhba revolt, Hadrian put down the rebellion and, according to the historical account, killed as many as half a million Jews; Jews were banned from the city on pain of death, except on Tisha B'Av.

In 614 the Sasanians took the city after 21 days; Byzantine chronicles say they and the Jews killed tens of thousands of Christians and destroyed churches, an episode historians have debated. In the early 11th century the Fatimid caliph al-Hakim ordered all churches destroyed. When the Crusaders took the city in July 1099 they massacred almost all of its Muslim and Jewish inhabitants. In 1219 the Ayyubid sultan of Damascus ordered the walls razed. In 1948 the Jewish population was besieged, civilians were killed on both sides, and Arab villages and districts of the west were taken and their residents displaced. After taking East Jerusalem in June 1967, Israel demolished the Moroccan Quarter, destroying 135 homes and 14 religious buildings.
sections.legacy:
Jerusalem is holy to three faiths. In Judaism the Temple Mount, site of Solomon's Temple and the Second Temple, is held to be the holiest site, and prayers are said facing it. Christians revere the city for its place in the life of Jesus, and the Church of the Holy Sepulchre holds the sites where, in Christian belief, he was crucified, buried and raised from the dead. Muslims hold that Muhammad travelled by night from Mecca to the farthest place of prayer, which Islamic scholars later understood as Jerusalem, and that Jerusalem was the first direction of prayer; the Dome of the Rock and the Qibli (al-Aqsa) Mosque stand on the compound.

The Old City, of less than 1 square kilometre, became a World Heritage Site in 1981. The city's status is disputed. Israel holds that Jerusalem is its complete and united capital, as its 1980 Jerusalem Law declares, while Palestinians regard East Jerusalem as the capital of the State of Palestine; most of the international community regards East Jerusalem as occupied Palestinian territory, and the Security Council called the 1980 law null and void. In 2024 the city had a population of 1,050,153, of whom in 2022 about 60 per cent were Jews and almost 40 per cent Palestinians.

summary: Jerusalem is a city of the Judaean Mountains that has been settled since about 3000 BCE and is holy to Judaism, Christianity and Islam. It has been besieged, destroyed and rebuilt many times under many rulers, from Canaanite and Judahite kings to Romans, Muslim dynasties, Crusaders, Ottomans and the British, and its political status is disputed today.
